fields.foundation: Maharaja Ranjit Singh, the founder of the Sikh Empire, was born in 1780 into the Sukerchakia Misl, one of the twelve Sikh confederacies that had governed the Punjab separately since Mughal authority broke down in the mid-eighteenth century. The Punjab in this period was a contested borderland, subject to repeated Afghan invasions under Ahmad Shah Durrani and his successors, and the Misls, though strong in the field, remained chronically disunited. Ranjit Singh's rise began when he was only eighteen. The Durrani ruler Zaman Shah withdrew from the Punjab, and in July 1799 Ranjit Singh seized Lahore from its Bhangi chiefs with the support of his mother-in-law Sada Kaur of the Kanhaiya Misl. He was formally proclaimed Maharaja on 12 April 1801, the day of Baisakhi, the spring harvest festival, which gave the proclamation a religious meaning, and in 1802 he took Amritsar, the spiritual centre of Sikhism. Over the following three decades he absorbed the remaining Misls through military pressure, marriage alliances and negotiated submission, and so united the Punjab for the first time as a single sovereign state. The Anglo-Sikh Treaty of 1806 and the Treaty of Amritsar of 1809 fixed the Sutlej River as the boundary between Sikh and East India Company spheres. They halted expansion to the east but spared the empire a direct confrontation with the British, and Ranjit Singh turned his armies north and west towards Multan, Kashmir and the Khyber frontier.
fields.socioeconomy: The Sikh Empire governed one of the most agriculturally productive regions of the subcontinent. The five rivers of the Punjab, the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, watered intensive cultivation of wheat, cotton and sugarcane across a densely populated countryside. Revenue administration followed a modified form of Mughal practice, with land assessed according to crop and yield and revenue collected through a hierarchy of kardars (revenue officers) and local intermediaries. The jagir system, the assignment of territorial revenues to military commanders and courtiers in lieu of salary, was the empire's principal means of rewarding its elite, though Ranjit Singh kept the most productive territories as khalsa (crown) land under direct management. Lahore was the capital and commercial hub, and its bazaars linked Central Asian caravan trade with the Himalayan passes and the markets of Hindustan. Amritsar, the spiritual centre of Sikhism, was also a major commercial entrepôt, trading in shawls, horses and dried fruits with Afghanistan, Kashmir and the wider Indian market. The population was religiously mixed, with a Muslim majority alongside Hindus, Sikhs and smaller communities. Ranjit Singh's administration followed a deliberate policy of inclusion and appointed Muslims, Hindus and Europeans to senior civil and military positions alongside the Sikh nobility.
fields.military: The Fauj-i-Ain, the regular army, was Ranjit Singh's chief institutional innovation and the instrument of Sikh expansion. He recognised that the traditional Khalsa cavalry, however effective in irregular warfare, could not match disciplined modern forces. From 1822 onwards he recruited veterans of the Napoleonic armies to drill his troops along European lines: the Frenchman Jean-François Allard raised a cavalry corps, the Italian Jean-Baptiste Ventura trained the infantry, and the Frenchman Claude Auguste Court reorganised the artillery. By the late 1830s the army's total strength is often estimated at around 100,000 men, regular and irregular, supported by a substantial artillery park, and many British observers regarded it as the strongest indigenous army in India. The conquest of Multan in 1818 secured southern Punjab, and the Sikh conquest of Kashmir in 1819 brought the valley under Lahore's authority. The occupation of Peshawar in 1834 extended the empire to the mouth of the Khyber Pass, giving Ranjit Singh a frontier with Afghanistan and a buffer against Afghan resurgence. That frontier was defended in 1837 at the Battle of Jamrud, where the general Hari Singh Nalwa was killed. The Battle of Nowshera (1823) against Afghan forces had already shown that disciplined infantry and artillery could work together with Khalsa horsemen. Such was the army's reputation that the East India Company kept to a cautious policy of non-interference beyond the Sutlej throughout Ranjit Singh's lifetime.
fields.governance: The Sikh Empire's government was centralised in the person of Ranjit Singh, whose authority was both secular and sacral. He ruled as Maharaja but presented himself as a servant of the Khalsa and the Sikh Panth, styling his government the Sarkar-i-Khalsa and issuing coins in the name of the Sikh Gurus rather than his own. The Lahore Darbar, the imperial court, was the centre of administration, and its senior offices, among them the wazir (chief minister), the diwan (finance minister) and the foreign minister, were held by a multiethnic and multireligious elite. Fakir Azizuddin, a Muslim, served as Ranjit Singh's principal foreign minister and envoy to the British; the Dogra Dhian Singh rose to become chief minister; and finance was managed successively by officials such as Diwan Bhawani Das, Diwan Ganga Ram and Diwan Dina Nath. Provincial government was delegated to governors (nazims) who were accountable to Lahore in theory but in practice had considerable autonomy, particularly in distant territories such as Kashmir and Peshawar. There was no codified legal system comparable to the Ottoman kanun or Mughal regulations; justice was administered through customary practice, sharia for Muslim subjects and ad hoc royal arbitration. These informal arrangements worked under a dominant personal sovereign. After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839 they failed, because no mechanism existed to settle the succession or restrain the competing ambitions of the Lahore Darbar's factions.
fields.impact: The Sikh Empire was a buffer between British India and the unsettled Afghan frontier at a critical stage of the Great Game, the rivalry between the British and Russian Empires for influence in Central and South Asia. Ranjit Singh's control of Peshawar and the approaches to the Khyber Pass denied Afghanistan a secure eastern frontier and complicated the strategic calculations of both Durrani and Barakzai rulers throughout the 1820s and 1830s. The empire's trade ranged from the shawl industry of Kashmir, whose fine pashmina was exported to European markets via Lahore and Delhi, to the horse trade of Central Asia and the grain markets of the Gangetic plain. Ranjit Singh's patronage changed the appearance of Amritsar. Under his sponsorship the upper storeys of the Harmandir Sahib were covered in gilded copper, work largely completed by around 1830, which gave the shrine its popular name, the Golden Temple. It remains the defining monument of Sikh civilisation. The empire was a Sikh-led, non-theocratic state that governed a Muslim-majority population with enough even-handedness to secure administrative loyalty, and later historians have often cited it as an example of pre-colonial plural government. Europeans who served at the Lahore court left detailed accounts, among them Allard's correspondence and the physician Johann Martin Honigberger's Thirty-five Years in the East, which are important primary sources for the period.
fields.decline: The Sikh Empire's collapse was among the fastest in this dataset: barely ten years separated the death of its founder from final annexation, and contemporaries struggled to account for it. Ranjit Singh died on 27 June 1839. He had named his eldest son Kharak Singh as heir but had built no institutions capable of managing the transition, and the Lahore Darbar was left to competing factions of Dogra courtiers, Sikh sardars and army commanders. Rulers followed one another quickly and violently. Kharak Singh died under suspicious circumstances in November 1840, and his son Nau Nihal Singh was fatally injured the same day by a collapsing gateway, in an accident that was equally suspicious. Sher Singh was assassinated in 1843, along with the chief minister Dhian Singh, and the five-year-old Duleep Singh was installed under the regency of his mother, Maharani Jind Kaur. The Khalsa army, unpaid and politically radicalised, increasingly dictated policy through its elected regimental committees (panchayats). Court leaders, among them the wazir Lal Singh and the commander-in-chief Tej Singh, are widely believed to have encouraged war with the British in the hope that defeat would break the army as a political force. The First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–1846) ended in Sikh defeat at Sobraon; the Treaty of Lahore stripped the empire of the Jullundur Doab and Kashmir, which the British then sold to the Dogra Gulab Singh for 7.5 million rupees under the Treaty of Amritsar (1846). The Second Anglo-Sikh War (1848–1849), triggered by risings at Multan and Hazara, ended with Lord Dalhousie's annexation of the entire Punjab on 29 March 1849, and the young Maharaja Duleep Singh was pensioned off and later taken to England.
fields.summary: The Sikh Empire showed that a Sikh-led, pluralist and militarily modernised state could arise after the Mughal collapse and briefly rival British India in military capacity. It lasted fifty years and fell suddenly, through the weakness of its institutions rather than military inferiority, and it is remembered as one of history's might-have-beens.
fields.teaser: The Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh was one of the last major powers to resist British expansion in India, known for its disciplined Khalsa army and religious tolerance.
fields.t0: Maharaja Ranjit Singh united the feuding Sikh Misls into a single Punjab state, ruling from Lahore from 1799.
fields.t1: Its European-drilled army was among the strongest in India, and it governed a Muslim-majority population with a mixed-faith court.
fields.t2: Without institutions to manage succession, it collapsed into court intrigue after 1839 and was annexed by Britain in 1849.
fields.dyk: Ranjit Singh had the upper storeys of the Harmandir Sahib covered in gilded copper, giving it its popular name: the Golden Temple.
